questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 8 equal parts. Point A sits at the end of the 4th part, counting from 0. A second number line, also from 0 to 1, is cut into 4 equal parts. Which fraction on the second number line lands on exactly the same point as A?
questions.explain: Count the equal spaces, not the marks: 4 of 8 spaces is half the line, and half of 4 equal parts is 2 parts, so 4/8 and 2/4 sit on the same point. Children who count the tick marks (including the one at 0) land one mark too far and pick the one that says 3/4.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 6 equal parts. Point B sits at the end of the 3rd part, counting from 0. Which other fraction names exactly the same point as B?
questions.explain: Point B is 3 of the 6 equal spaces from 0, which is 3/6, and 3/6 is the same distance as 1/2, so both names land on one point. The trap is counting the marks instead of the spaces: there are 7 marks and B is the 4th one, which makes children write 4/6 or 4/7.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 3 equal parts. Point C sits at the end of the 1st part, counting from 0. A second number line, also from 0 to 1, is cut into 9 equal parts. Which fraction on the second number line lands on exactly the same point as C?
questions.explain: Point C is 1/3 of the way along, and each third holds 3 of the ninths, so C is also 3/9 - the same point with a different name. Children who count marks instead of spaces make C the 4th mark and write 4/9, or the 2nd of 4 marks and write 2/4.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 10 equal parts. Point D sits at the end of the 2nd part, counting from 0. A second number line, also from 0 to 1, is cut into 5 equal parts. Which fraction on the second number line lands on exactly the same point as D?
questions.explain: Point D is 2/10 of the way from 0, and two tenths make one fifth, so the matching point on the fifths line is 1/5 - the end of the first equal part. Counting marks instead of spaces makes that first part look like the 2nd mark, which is why 2/5 tempts so many children.

questions.question: A number line from 0 to 1 is divided into twelfths. Which fraction lands on exactly the same point as 2/3?
questions.explain: Each third is split into 4 twelfths, so 2/3 covers 2 x 4 = 8 twelfths and lands on 8/12. Counting the twelfth marks from 0 (instead of the spaces between them) pushes the dot one mark too far and gives the one that says 9/12.

questions.question: A juice jug has a scale from 0 L to 1 L divided into 10 equal parts, and Ella fills it to the 6/10 L mark. A second jug has a scale from 0 L to 1 L divided into 5 equal parts. Which mark on the second jug shows the same amount of juice?
questions.explain: Two tenths make one fifth, so 6/10 L is 3 groups of two tenths, which is 3/5 L - the same point on both scales. Children who count the fifth marks starting at 0 slide up one and choose the one that says 4/5.

questions.question: Ravi wants to mark 3/4 on a number line that runs from 0 to 1 and is already divided into 8 equal parts. Counting the equal parts from 0, where should his dot go?
questions.explain: Each fourth equals 2 of the eighths, so 3/4 equals 6/8 and the dot belongs at the end of the 6th equal part. The common trap is counting marks: children stop at the 3rd mark (2/8) or count the mark at 0 first and land at the 7th part.

questions.question: On a number line from 0 to 1, which pair of fractions lands on exactly the same point?
questions.explain: Two sixths and one third cover the same distance from 0, because each third is made of 2 sixths, so those two names share one point. Fractions like 3/4 and 4/5 only look alike because each number went up by one - that is mark counting, not equal spaces, and their points are different.

questions.question: Jayden's number line runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 4 equal parts. To show 3/4 he counts the vertical marks, calling the mark at 0 the first one, and puts his dot on the third mark. Which statement is true?
options: His dot landed on 2/4, which is the same point as 1/2, not 3/4.
His dot landed on 3/5, because the line has 5 marks in all.
His dot landed on 3/4, because the third mark always shows 3/4.
His dot landed on 3/4, the same point as 6/8.
questions.explain: The marks are 0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 1, so the third mark is 2/4 - the same point as 1/2 - while 3/4 is the fourth mark, at the end of the 3rd equal space. Always count the equal spaces you travel from 0, never the marks you pass.

questions.question: A seawall path has a 1 km section with a marker every 100 m, starting at the 0 m marker and ending at the 1000 m marker. Priya has walked 3/5 of this section. Which marker is she standing at?
questions.explain: One fifth of 1 km is 200 m, so 3/5 is 600 m, which is also the 6/10 point - the same spot named two ways. Counting markers instead of the 200 m spaces (calling the 0 m marker the first fifth) lands wrongly on 400 m.

questions.question: Amir and Sofia each drew a number line from 0 to 1 the same length. Amir cut his into 6 equal parts and put a dot at the end of the 4th part. Sofia cut hers into 9 equal parts and put a dot at the end of the 6th part. Do their dots land on the same point?
options: No - 6/9 must be farther from 0 than 4/6, because 6 is bigger than 4.
No - Amir's dot is on the 5th mark and Sofia's is on the 7th mark, so they cannot match.
Yes - both dots are 2/3 of the way from 0 to 1.
No - Amir's line has fewer parts, so his dot has to be closer to 1.
questions.explain: 4/6 and 6/9 both simplify to 2/3, so on lines of the same length the two dots sit on one point. Bigger numerators do not mean farther along, and counting marks instead of equal spaces makes matching points look different.

questions.question: On a number line from 0 to 1 cut into 12 equal parts, Leo puts a dot at the end of the 9th part. Which fraction lands on the same point, and how does that point compare with the benchmark 1/2?
options: 5/6, and it is greater than 1/2, because Leo's dot is on the 10th mark.
questions.explain: Nine twelfths is three groups of three twelfths, so the dot is also 3/4, and since 1/2 would be 6/12, the dot sits past the halfway benchmark. Watch the mark-counting trap: the dot is the 10th mark but only the 9th equal space, so it is 9/12, not 10/12 or 5/6.
